title: Val Head – Purpose and Style: Using motion with meaning in interfaces
summary: Val Head (Adobe design advocate, author of 'Designing Interface Animation') argues that good UI animation always combines a user-centred purpose with a style that fits the rest of the design. She walks through three purposes (continuity / spatial mental model, feedback, directing attention) with real product examples, then gives five choreography rules: accelerate into exits, decelerate into entrances, overlap groups, animate similar things similarly, and match velocities rather than durations; the Q&A adds prefers-reduced-motion.

insights.insight: Continuity builds a spatial map: on small screens much of the interface lives off-screen, and the direction something enters from tells the user where it lives and where to find it again (Cotton Bureau: navigation slides in from the left, cart from the right). If it just appeared, users would have to work out where it came from; seeing it travel removes that cognitive load.
insights.quote: it creates this mental, almost physical map of an interface
insights.visual: Cotton Bureau site projected on stage with the dark navigation drawer slid in from the left edge over the orange product page.

insights.insight: Containment through motion: Google Fonts' colour palette scales, rotates slightly and fades out of the little paint-bucket icon and goes back into it, so the user feels the palette 'lives inside' that button. Small scale + rotation + opacity from a source element is enough to imply a physical origin and home.
insights.visual: Google Fonts directory with the paint-bucket control at top right opened into round colour swatches (black, red, yellow, blue) above the type specimens.

insights.insight: Feedback can be rewarding, not just utilitarian: Medium's clap bursts small particles and pops a counter, which makes the action feel tactile and worth repeating. Even complex feedback must keep pace with the user (Google Docs' drag-a-stack-into-a-folder animation is rich and 3D yet never makes you wait). Layer feedback across channels (motion + colour + text).
insights.visual: Medium 'Show your support' block with the cursor on the green clap button and the clap count beside it.

insights.insight: Motion is the design tool with the loudest 'outside voice': the gap between subtle and in-your-face is far smaller than with colour. Scale the intensity to how much the user should care: CodePen's Save button shakes harder and harder only because losing work matters, while Stripe rings its notification bell once and adds a badge. The same shake on every nav button would be unbearable.
insights.quote: animation is the one most likely to be speaking with its outside voice
insights.visual: Stage slide 'Direct Attention: leading the eye and calling attention to changes and important items'.

insights.insight: Physical easing rules: things should accelerate into an exit (ease-in when leaving) and slow down before stopping (ease-out for entrances). An element that arrives at full speed and stops dead looks wrong; decelerating into place reads as natural and unremarkable, which is the goal.
insights.visual: Slide 'Slow down before stopping' with a teal square easing into place and the tip 'use ease out easing for entrances'.

insights.insight: Overlap groups of actions (stagger): instead of bringing items in one after another, start the next before the previous finishes. Only the start offsets change, yet the group forms a smooth arc and the whole sequence finishes sooner; her 'number one tip' for looking professional.
insights.quote: the next one starts before the one before is finished
insights.visual: Slide 'Overlap groups of actions': two teal panels, the left one (sequential) still empty while the right one (overlapped) already shows its first dots fading in.

insights.insight: Similar objects should animate similarly. Giving each thumbnail a different entrance to make it 'interesting' makes users wonder whether the items are different kinds of things. Consistent motion patterns are a usability feature, not a lack of creativity.
insights.visual: Slide 'Similar objects should animate similarly': on the left three thumbnails arrive the same way beside a photo; on the right a contrasting version.

insights.insight: Match velocities, not durations. A blanket '200 ms for everything' makes an element travelling far move much faster than one travelling a short way, so related objects stop looking related. Let longer moves take longer so the visible top speed matches.
insights.quote: matching velocity visually is gonna be better than matching those durations
insights.visual: Slide 'Match velocities, not duration': two squares travelling different distances in each panel, caught mid-move.

apply_to_wael: Give every surface a fixed home and always enter/leave from it: the level and subject pickers rise from Wael's speech bubble or the bottom edge, the account sheet slides up from the bottom, and the town map is 'below' the island so the camera descends to it. Same origin every time, so the map of the game forms on its own.

Stagger the content of each step: level chips and subject badges appear with a ~40-60 ms offset (overlapping, ease-out), all with the same motion since they are the same kind of thing; answer options of the 3 questions likewise. Keep the total under ~400 ms so nobody waits.

Make exits ease-in (accelerate away) and entrances ease-out/spring (decelerate in), and size durations by distance: a short chip nudge ~150-200 ms, a full camera move over the island ~600-900 ms, so the town and the UI look like they move at one consistent speed.

Spend 'loud' motion only where it matters: one celebratory burst on the result screen, a gentle single ring/pulse to draw the eye to 'Create account', and a short shake only for a wrong answer; everything else stays quiet. Respect prefers-reduced-motion by swapping camera moves for crossfades.
